opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is to look at the history of intelligence on this planet. If you think about evolution, multicellular life has been around for something like five hundred million years, and for almost all of that time animals were getting very good at perceiving the world, moving through it, manipulating objects, avoiding predators, finding food. Language, by contrast, is a very recent addition, maybe a few hundred thousand years at most. So language sits on top of an enormous foundation of perceptual and motor competence. It's the icing, not the cake.

And you see the same thing in child development. A baby is looking around, reaching, grasping, putting things in their mouth, crawling, dropping toys off the high chair to see what happens. They are running experiments on the physical world well before they produce their first words. When language comes, it gets grounded in all of that experience. When a child learns the word "cup," they already know what a cup is: you can hold it, it contains things, it can tip over and spill.

Now, current large language models have gone about it the other way around. They've learned from text, which is this incredibly compressed, distilled residue of human experience. And they're remarkably impressive, I don't want to take anything away from that. But there's a real question of grounding. Much of what we know about the world is never written down because it's too obvious to say. Nobody writes "if you push a glass off the table, it falls and may break" because every human knows it. That kind of common sense about space, objects, forces, and agency comes from embodied interaction, and I think it's very hard to get fully from text alone.

So my view is that if we want AI systems that truly understand the world, that can act in it as robots, and that have the robustness and generality we see in animals and humans, we should take seriously the idea of building up from perception and action. Learn from vision, from touch, from moving around and interacting, and then let language attach to that grounded representation. I'm not saying language is unimportant. It's tremendously important, especially for culture and for transmitting knowledge between people. But I think the path to general intelligence runs through the physical world first.

r001.rationale: The response says language is grounded in physical experience, but it does not identify physical experience as a source of metaphors through which language develops.

r002.rationale: It proposes grounding language in perception and action, but does not say that physical metaphors make AI language abilities easier to build.

r003.rationale: It describes babies reaching, grasping, crawling, and exploring the world before they produce their first words.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that this is the order in which nature did it. If you look at evolution, we have had animals with vision and locomotion and manipulation for something like five hundred million years. Language, in anything like the human sense, is maybe a hundred thousand years old. So the overwhelming bulk of the computational machinery in the brain was shaped by the problem of perceiving the world and acting in it, and language came very late, riding on top of all that.

And it's not just a historical accident. If you look at a child, the first couple of years of life are spent learning about objects, about space, about what happens when you push something or drop something, about other people and what they intend. All of that happens before the child has any meaningful command of language. When the words do come, they attach to concepts that are already there. The child knows what a cup is, what falling is, long before they can say "cup" or "fall." So the meaning is grounded in sensorimotor experience, and language is a labeling and communication system built on top of that grounding.

Now, the reason I think this matters for AI is that if you start with language alone, you're learning from the shadows, so to speak. Text is a very compressed, very lossy record of human experience. It leaves out exactly the things that are obvious to everyone, because nobody bothers to write them down. Nobody writes that if you let go of a glass it falls, or that you can't walk through a wall. Large language models have done remarkably well, far better than I would have predicted, but I think they inherit this weakness. Their understanding of the physical and social world is secondhand.

Whereas if you build a system that has to perceive, has to move, has to manipulate objects and deal with the consequences of its actions, it is forced to acquire that commonsense knowledge directly. The world is the teacher, and the world doesn't let you cheat. So my bet, and I've held this view for a long time, is that the path to robust intelligence goes through the body and through perception first. Language then becomes enormously powerful, but as a layer on top of something that already understands what it is talking about.

r001.rationale: The response says sensorimotor experience grounds concepts that language later labels, but it does not identify physical experience as a source of metaphors.

r002.rationale: It presents language as a layer built on physical understanding, but does not communicate the criterion’s claim about physical metaphors grounding language abilities.

r003.rationale: It describes children learning about objects, space, and actions before meaningful language, and notes that locomotion and manipulation predate language in evolution.

astra-6.text:
Because physical intelligence gives you a grounding in the world. Before a child can speak, the child can see, reach for things, pick them up, and learn what happens when something is dropped. There is already a considerable amount of intelligence there, even though there is no language yet.

Think about what it takes to pick up a cup. You have to understand its shape, where to grasp it, how much force to apply, and what will happen as you move it. Much of that knowledge is learned through perception and action. You don't acquire it simply by hearing descriptions of cups.

Language is enormously powerful because it lets us communicate and learn from other people's experiences. But I favor starting with physical intelligence because it provides something for language to refer to. You first build an understanding of objects, actions, and consequences, and then language can build on that foundation.

r002.rationale: It says physical intelligence provides a foundation that language can build on, grounding language in an understanding of objects, actions, and consequences.

r003.rationale: It describes a child reaching for and picking up things before speaking, showing motor skills developing without language.

sol-6.1.text:
My view is that perception and action provide the foundation on which language builds. If you look at a child, long before the child can speak, it can see, move, pick things up, and learn what happens when it acts on the world. Language comes into a system that already has some understanding of objects, space, and cause and effect.

That matters because words refer to things and experiences. You can describe a chair in language, but understanding a chair also involves knowing that you can sit on it, that it supports your weight, and that you can move around it. Those are things you learn through interaction.

So I favor starting with perception and action, and then bringing in language as a very powerful way of communicating and learning. I don’t think language is unimportant. I think it becomes much more meaningful when it is grounded in an understanding of the physical world.

r002.rationale: It presents perception and action as a foundation for language and says grounding makes language more meaningful, but does not say this makes AI language abilities easier to build.

r003.rationale: It says that before speaking, a child can move and pick things up, clearly asserting motor abilities can develop without language.
